entry.title: summer rolls with pork
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for deliciously simple rice paper rolls with versatile topping choices for a fun hands-on meal with creamy peanut dipping sauce on the side.

Materials

  • Freezer bag
  • Saute pan
  • Saucepan
  • Silicone spatula
  • Colander
  • Wide bowl
  • 3 Plates

Reagents

Meat and marinade

||Ingredient|Amount|Preparation| |:—|:—|:—|:—| ||Water|2 Cups|None| ||Soy sauce|1 Cup|None| ||Fish Sauce|2 Tbsp|None| ||Black pepper flakes|1 Tbsp|None| ||Optional: Cayenne|1 Tbsp|None| ||Neutral oil|1 Tbsp|None| ||Pork neck or loin|2 lbs|Thinly sliced, fresh or frozen|


Fresh toppings

||Ingredient|Amount|Preparation| |:—|:—|:—|:—| ||Crunchy peanut butter|1/2 cup|May be substituted with regular peanut butter and coarsely chopped peanuts| ||Lime juice or rice vinegar|1 Tbsp|None| ||Optional: Sambal|1 Tbsp|None|


Fresh toppings

||Ingredient|Amount|Preparation| |:—|:—|:—|:—| ||Vermicelli noodles|1 serving|None| ||Rice paper|1 packet of at least 8|None| ||Do chua||None| ||Lettuce|2 small heads|Washed and dried| ||Mint|3-5 sprigs|Washed and dried| ||Thai basil|3-5 sprigs|Washed and dried| ||Cucumber|1/2 cucumber|Washed and cut into matchsticks| ||Bell pepper|1 pepper|Washed and cut into matchsticks| ||Optional: Green mango|1 mango|Washed and cut into matchsticks|


Procedure

Marinate pork

Hands-on: 10 mins| Incubation: 1-12 h

  1. Add marinade ingredients to a freezer bag and gently shake to mix.
  2. Add thinly sliced pork to the freezer bag.
  3. Mix pork and marinade to ensure even coating.
  4. Allow meat to marinate for at least 1 hour to overnight in the fridge.
    • If marinating frozen meat, allow additional time for defrosting, at least 4 hours.
Cook pork

Hands-on: 20 mins

  1. Reserve 4 Tbsp of marinade for the peanut sauce. The rest may be poured out or reserved for another recipe.
  2. Heat saute pan to medium-heat. Add neutral cooking oil.
  3. Cook pork slices in small batches depending on pan size to prevent crowding the pan.
  4. Cook pork slice for 1 min before flipping and cooking the other side for 30s.
  5. Place finished pork slices in a plate.
Peanut sauce
  1. Add reserved marinade to a saucepan and bring to a boil.
  2. Add peanut butter and stir to mix. Sauce will be thick.
  3. Turn off the heat.
  4. Add lime juice and sambal if using.
  5. Scoop sauce into small dipping bowls.
Cook Vermicelli
  1. Bring 4 cups of water to a boil in a saucepan.
  2. Add vermicelli noodles to the boiling water and cook for 8 mins or as indicated by the package.
  3. Place colander over the sink. Pour cooked vermicelli into the colander, allowing the water to drain.
  4. Briefly rinse the cooked vermicelli with cold water, tossing to ensure even cooling.
  5. Place the colander over a plate.
Assembling the Summer Rolls
  1. Add water to the wide bowl.
  2. Roll a piece of rice paper 2 times (720o), ensuring there are no dry spots on the paper.
  3. Place the rice paper on your plate.
  4. Place a lettuce leaf in the bottom third of the rice paper. This will serve as the backbone for your roll.
  5. Add vermicelli, the cooked pork, do chua, mint, basil, cucumber, bell pepper and any additional desired ingredients in the lettuce basket. Don’t overstuff your roll or it will fall apart!
  6. Grab the bottom edge of the rice paper and pull it over the ingredients, tightly covering them.
  7. Fold in the left and right edges to seal in the ingredients.
  8. Finish rolling the rice paper tightly. The rice paper will seal the roll by itself.
  9. Your finished summer roll is ready to be dipped in the peanut sauce and enjoyed!
Yield 8 rolls.
Storage Wrap any leftover rolls individually in cling wrap. Store in the fridge for up to 3 days.


Discussion

Summer rolls with a side of peanut sauce. Photo from Unsplash.

Summer rolls are an easy way to introduce friends and family to the simple freshness of Vietnamese cuisine. The simple art of building your own roll adds a touch of personalization that caters to all taste buds. In this recipe, I mix a combination of fresh, crunchy and chewy textures which all come together in a neat little package to be dipped in a crunchy, nutty sauce.

Protein Variations

In this recipe, sauteed pork is used as the protein. However, feel free to substitute with other proteins. Some traditional options are shrimp, BBQ meat and tofu strips. The protein not only provides additional nutritional value, but serves as the backbone of the flavor profile and texture. The chewiness of the protein complements the other textures in the roll.

Topping Variations

Most of the fresh toppings add a bit of crunch to the roll to create a fun and exciting mouthfeel. Other toppings to try are carrot matchsticks, cilantro, bean sprouts, purple cabbage, radishes, pickled mushrooms, bok choy or avocado; ordered from traditional to more creative. Summer rolls are especially refreshing when making them similar to how one would pair fruit salads, with plenty of mangoes, peaches, watermelon, pear, cucumber and mint.

Most importantly, use ingredients that are available to you either in the markets or your own garden.

Dipping Sauce Variations

My preferred dipping sauce is a thick peanut sauce that can be scooped with my summer rolls - it especially goes well with savory proteins. For a lighter profile, a traditional fish sauce blend may be used instead, mixing a 1:1:2 ratio of fish sauce:sugar:water and adding a splash of vinegar or do chua for brightness. This variation is more runny than the peanut sauce so be mindful of drips!
entry.summary: a simple rice paper roll served with creamy peanut sauce

entry.title: do chua (vietnamese pickled carrots & daikon)
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for refreshingly crisp Vietnamese pickled carrot and daikon side dish.

Inspired by Hungry Huy’s recipe.

Materials

  • Colander
  • Optional: Paper towels or cheese cloth
  • Mandolin or vegetable peeler
  • Saucepan
  • Measuring cups
  • 2 26 oz Sterilized glass jars

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Carrots 1/2 lb Washed and dried
Daikon radish 1/2 lb Washed and dried
Salt 2 Tbsp None
Water (Filtered preferred) 1 Cup None
Distilled vinegar 1/2 Cup None
Granulated sugar 1/8 Cup None


Procedure

Prepare Vegetables

Hands-on: 30 mins | Incubation: 15 mins

  1. Optional: Line a colander with paper towels or cheese cloth.
  2. Cut carrots and daikon into matchsticks using a mandolin or vegetable peeler. Thinner cuts will pickle faster.
  3. Place matchsticks in the colander.
  4. Sprinkle salt over the veggies and toss to evenly coat. Let sit for 15 mins to pull moisture out of the veggies.
  5. Rinse vegetables to remove salt.
  6. Squeeze vegetables with cheese cloth if using to remove excess moisture.
  7. Add vegetables to jars.
Prepare Pickling Solution

Hands-on: 10 mins

  1. Boil water in a saucepan.
  2. Add vinegar and sugar, stirring until sugar dissolves.
  3. Pour pickling solution in the jars with vegetables evenly.
  4. Optional: Add filtered water to submerge the veggies.
Ferment Do Chua

Incubation: 2-5 days

  1. Screw on jar lids tightly.
    • As the contents of the jar cools, the jar lid will pop to indicate that a seal has formed. Seal may be tested by pushing the button on the lid - if it pops, seal is compromised.
  2. Store jars in a cool, dark spot for 2-5 days.
  3. Bubbles will start to form after 1-2 days.
  4. Store jar in the fridge 1 day after bubbles form.
  5. Serve on the side or as a topping to main dishes.
Yield 2 26 oz jars.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 months. Ensure pop is heard after first opening. Use within 1 month after opening.


Discussion

Vietnamese banh mi stuffed with do chua. Photo from Unsplash.

As a refreshing and versatile Vietnamese side dish, do chua can be found in many dishes which feature rich or heavy ingredients to balance the flavors. Do chua literally translates to “sour stuff” funnily enough. The sweet, satisfying crunch of the pickled veggies along with the fragrant, slightly tangy pickling juice, makes this one of my favorite side dishes. Initially, this recipe was prepared for long-term storage of a carrot harvest and evolved into a tradition, where a fresh batch is always found in the fridge.

Main dishes

The first dish I made with my fresh pickled carrots and radish was summer rolls. Using a stretchy circle of rice paper, fresh ingredients are wrapped – including do chua for a tangy crunch. As a rule of thumb, anywhere fish sauce is used, do chua can be used to either contrast the strong flavor or even added to the sauce to brighten it.

Other dishes I’ve made to go with the do chua are banh mi (stuffed sandwich with a rich slathering of liver pate and butter), banh xeo (savory crispy crepes with pork belly and shrimp), bo tai chanh (tangy and pungent lemon-marinated beef carpaccio) and bun thit nuong (vermicelli noodles with BBQ pork). These dishes all revolve around a fatty ingredient, where the do chua helps lighten the flavor and mouthfeel.

entry.title: fermented habanero sauce
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for a fiery, fruity fermented hot sauce with a touch of tart plum and smokey paprika — perfect for adding heat and complexity to your dishes

Materials

  • Recommended: food-safe powder-free gloves
  • Knife and cutting board
  • Small bowl and spoon
  • Sterilized jar
  • Pickling weight or cabbage leaf
  • Plate with rim
  • Strainer and bowl
  • Food processor or blender
  • Bottle with pour spout

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Habanero peppers 3/4-1 Cup Washed
Carrot 1 Carrot Washed, cut into matchsticks
Shallots or yellow onion 1/2 Cup Diced
Garlic 4-8 Cloves Sliced
(Filtered) Water 2 Cups None
Kosher salt 14 g None
Optional: Sauerkraut pickling juice 2 Tbsp None
Recommended: Plum 1/2 Plum Wash and skin peeled
Optional: Salt To taste None
Optional: Smoked paprika To taste None


Procedure

Prepare Habaneros

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Don gloves, wash gloves with soap.
  2. Using a knife and cutting board, slice habaneros in half. Remove seeds and stem.
  3. Slice habaneros into thin strips - the thinner, the faster the ferment.
  4. Set aside in a small bowl. Discard gloves.
Prepare Pickling Brine

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Add salt to the water to make a 3% brine.
  2. In a jar, add carrot matchsticks, diced shallots and sliced garlic. Using a spoon, add the sliced habaneros to the jar.
  3. Top off with brine, making sure all vegetables are submerged.
  4. Add the pickling weight or cabbage leaf to prevent veggies from floating.
  5. Fill rest of the jar with the brine. Add sauerkraut pickling juice if using.
Ferment

Incubation: 7-60 days

  1. Place jar in a cool, dark spot over a plate with a rim.
  2. Close the lid partway to allow fermentation gases to escape. Ferment for 7-60 days.
    • Bubbles should start to form a day after fermenting if using sauerkraut pickling juice as a starter or within 3 days.
    • Longer fermentation mellows the spice in the habaneros.
Blend Sauce

Hands-on: 10 mins

  1. Strain the fermented vegetables over a bowl to reserve the pickling liquid.
  2. Add the fermented vegetables minus the cabbage to a food processor or blender. Add 1/4 to 1 cup of pickling liquid to the food processor depending on preferred thickness of the sauce.
  3. Add plum, smoked paprika, salt and any additional toppings to taste.
  4. Blend vegetables until a smooth sauce forms.
  5. Add sauce to sterilized glass jar or bottle with an open pour spout.
  6. Store in the fridge loosely covered as sauce will continue to ferment.
Yield 14 oz.
Storage Store in the fridge for up to 3 months. Keep loosely covered.


Discussion

Habaneros fresh from the market. Photo from Unsplash.

I made this fermented habanero hot sauce as a way to enjoy a batch of fresh habaneros from the market in an enjoyable way. I fermented my batch for just a couple days under a month. Once fermented, the initial taste was tangy and bright up front, with a manageable, lingering heat. The sauce was also surprisingly sweet, but I wanted to add a bit of tartness with some plums that were on sale and smokiness with a pinch of paprika.

If you love this sauce, check out the yuzu habanero jelly for another creative twist.

Fermentation

The bacteria that are found on the peels of root vegetables like carrots and potatoes or leafy vegetables like cabbage are responsible for starting the fermentation process. Those bacteria are dormant in sauerkraut pickling juice, but can be reactivated when taken out of the cold of the fridge and provided carbohydrates from the fresh vegetables through a process called Lactic Acid Fermentation. The fermentation process also moderates the spice of the habaneros though will not completely remove it.

Variations

The usual habanero pairing is mango or strawberry, a sweet, tart fruit to contrast the burning spice of habanero. I had plums on hand and found the flesh to be refreshing and slightly tart. Feel free to get creative with whatever fruit you’ve got lying around! Other pairings are kiwi, pineapple and pomegranate.

In addition to the fruit added after fermentation, we added carrots to the pickle to help jump start the fermentation with the bacteria usually found on carrot skin. The mildness of carrots will also balance the spiciness of the habanero. Other neutral vegetables can be used in place of carrot such as bell peppers.

Spice Level

Habaneros bring serious heat, but with fermentation and fruity additions, they become surprisingly approachable. These peppers have a rating of 100-350k Scoville Heat Units (SCU) which is on the spicier side, since it was readily available to me for free at a farmer’s market. The resulting heat in the jelly was surprisingly bearable (coming from someone with a mild spice tolerance). Fermenting the peppers will reduce the heat, so the fermenting time may be adjusted based on desired spice level. Yes, my tongue and mouth still burned, but it was nothing like the heat I felt after slicing the habaneros, washing my hands (3 times!) and touching my face - please be careful when handling peppers!

For comparison, here are the SCUs of some commonly eaten peppers:

Pepper Spiciness (SCU)
Bell pepper 0
Jalapeno pepper 2.5-10k
Cayenne pepper 25-50K
Thai chilies 50-100k
Habanero pepper 100k-350K

entry.title: garlic confit sauce (mojo de ajo)
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for spreadable liquid gold - garlic confit. The confit process, or low-heat frying, allows the flavors to develop as the garlic cloves fry into a golden brown.

Materials

  • Oven safe pan
  • Blender or food processor
  • 3 Sterilized glass jars

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Garlic 50 cloves, about 4 heads, or enough to cover the bottom of the pan Peeled
Olive oil 1-2 Cups, or enough to cover the garlic cloves None
Optional: Fresh Rosemary 3-5 Sprigs Washed and dried
Optional: Fresh Thyme 3-5 Sprigs Washed and dried
Optional: Black peppercorn 3-5 Peppercorns None
Optional: Chili flakes 1 Tbsp None
An acid (lemon juice, orange juice or vinegar) 1/2 cup None
Salt 1/2 Tbsp None
Optional: Fresh Cilantro 1 Cup Washed and dried


Procedure

Confit the Garlic

Hands-on: 10 mins | Incubation: 1-1.5 h

  1. Preheat oven to 300oF.
  2. Add garlic cloves to the pan in a single layer.
  3. Add toppings if using.
  4. Add olive oil until all cloves and toppings are submerged.
  5. Bake at 300oF for 1-1.5h or until garlic is golden brown.
  6. Serve the fresh garlic confit and oil spread over toast or proteins.
Make the Garlic Sauce

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Add the garlic, your acid, salt and any toppings to a blender. Mixture will be thick.
  2. Stream in the reserved olive oil until desired consistency.
    • Excess oil may be stored in an air-tight container in the fridge for up to 1 month
  3. Serve the garlic sauce over toast or proteins.
Yield 2-3 10 oz jars.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 month or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Sauce will separate and oil layer may solidify, so scoop from both layers.


Discussion

Garlic cloves sizzling in a pan with olive oil. Photo from Unsplash.

The sauce is a perfect addition to toast or any strongly-flavored protein dish. With the pungent initial bite of garlic, followed by mellow notes of the added herbs and spices, this sauce is a garlic-lover’s dream. A flavorful oil is also produced, which may be drizzled over pastas or soups.

Safety

This recipe is a way of preserving large amounts of garlic cloves for long-term storage (thank you Costco-sized bag of peeled garlic). Garlic stored in oil has a short shelf life due to the anaerobic, low-acid environment which is ideal for Clostridium botulinum to reproduce. I adapt the Brazilian mojo de ajo recipe with its use of an acid to prevent the ideal environment for C. botulinum. This adds a bright splash of flavor to complement the caramelized garlic flavor of the confit. Feel free to use any citrus on hand - I personally love the combination of orange juice and yuzu extract. The prepared garlic sauce has a long shelf-life in the refrigerator, though it will disappear very quickly!

Variations

Garlic is an ingredient that it used in dishes worldwide. The toppings added to the oil help develop more flavor as it confits and that flavor profile can be changed to suit your dish. I opted for a bright and herbal sauce that works well with a variety of dishes - my personal favorites being sandwiches and steaks. The sauce can be made spicier with the addition of chili flakes, ginger and cinnamon. Or another variation could be more suitable for pastas with the addition of fresh oregano and basil.

Olive oil is used to impart a light profile, but heavier animal fats can be used as well to create a smokier oil. I have tried this recipe using leftover fat from frying Chinese sausage, lap cheong, and adding the rest of the volume in olive oil to submerge the garlic cloves. This produced a sauce with complex layers of flavor which can’t be achieved using olive oil alone.
entry.summary: a Brazilian-inspired take on garlic confit

entry.title: strawberry cinnamon coffee cake
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for a dense coffee cake with swirls of cinnamon, pockets of fresh strawberries topped with gooey, salty cheese.

Heavily inspired by Sally’s recipe with some substitutions. I used non-fat greek yogurt instead of full-fat sour cream; added salt to the cheese topping instead of sugar; opted for no icing.

Materials

  • 3 Large bowls
  • Cling wrap
  • Colander
  • Recommended: Stand mixer with paddle attachment
  • Silicone spatula
  • Optional: Angled spatula
  • 9” Round springform pan
  • 9” Round parchment paper
  • Aluminum foil to cover 9” springform pan
  • BBQ skewer

Reagents

Cinnamon crumb
  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Brown sugar 1/3 Cup or 67g None
Cinnamon 2 Tsp None
All purpose flour 1/2 cup or 63 g Spooned and leveled
Butter 3 Tbsp or 43 g Cold, cut into small cubes


Cheese topping
  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Mascarpone cheese (may substitute with cream cheese) 8 oz or 226 g Softened at room temperature
Kosher salt 1/4 Tsp None


Cake batter
  Ingredient Amount Preparation
All purpose flour 1 and 1/3 Cups or 166 g Spooned & Leveled
Baking powder 1 Tsp None
Baking soda 1/2 Tsp None
Kosher salt 1/2 Tsp None
Unsalted butter 1/2 Cup or 113 g Softened at room temperature
Granulated sugar 3/4 Cup or 150 g None
Large Eggs 2 Eggs Room temperature
Vanilla Extract 2 Tsp None
Greek yogurt (non-fat or full-fat) 1/2 cup or 120 g Room temperature
Strawberries (may substitute with other berries) 1 Cup Fresh or frozen


Procedure

Prepare Crumb Topping

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. In a large bowl, combine brown sugar, flour and cinnamon.
  2. Add the cold butter and press between fingers to create small flat disks of butter. Continue pressing the butter until pea-sized crumbs remain.
  3. Cover the bowl and place in fridge to chill.
Prepare Cheese Topping

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. In a large bowl, add the softened cheese and salt.
  2. Whisk until combined. The cheese will be thick.
Prepare Berries

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. If using fresh berries, wash in a colander and briefly dry.
  2. Cut the berries into 1/2 x 1/2” cubes.
    • The size does not need to be precise. At this size, strawberries will still have a slight crunch after baking.
  3. Set prepared berries aside.
Prepare Batter

Hands-on: 10 mins

  1. In a large bowl, sift flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt. Briefly mix with a silicone spatula. Set dry ingredients aside.
  2. In a stand mixer, ddd butter and granulated sugar. Mix on high until creamy, about 2 mins.
  3. Add 1 egg at a time, mixing until fully incorporated.
  4. Add vanilla extract and greek yogurt, mixing briefly.
  5. Scrape down the sides of the bowl.
  6. On low, add half of the dry ingredients until incorporated. Add the other half of the dry ingredients. Mix until incorporated.
  7. Add prepared berries and fold in with silicone spatula.
Bake Cake

Hands-on: 10 mins | Incubation: 1.5 h

  1. Pre-heat oven at 350oF and grease 9” springform pan.
  2. In the greased springform pan, spread about 1/2 to 2/3 of the cake batter to cover the bottom of the pan with the angled spatula, if using.
  3. Sprinkle half the crumb on top of the batter
  4. Spread the rest of the cake batter.
    • Batter will be thick and difficult to spread, but when baked, it will spread to form a complete layer.
  5. Spread cheese topping. Again, cheese will be thick, but will spread with heat.
  6. Sprinkle the rest of the crumb layer over the cheese topping.
  7. Bake cake at 350oF for 60-65 mins or until center no longer jiggles. Halfway through bake time, lightly wrap aluminum foil over the springform pan.
    • Test cake doneness with a BBQ skewer through the center of the cake – it should come out mostly clean.
  8. Cool cake for at least 30 mins at room temperature before removing the springform pan.
  9. Serve generous slices with tea or coffee.
Yield 8 servings.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 3 months.


Discussion

Coffee cake topped with crumbs and berries. Photo from Unsplash.

When I found strawberries half-off at my local grocery store, I knew I needed to bake a strawberry cake. The sourness of the discounted strawberries complemented the sweet batter, the subtle spiciness of the cinnamon swirls and the saltiness of the cheese topping. The cake is dense but very moist, owing to the addition of greek yogurt (my favorite ingredient to look for in a cake recipe!). This recipe uses readily available ingredients in my pantry and I encourage you to as well, by understanding how certain substitutions affect the cake chemistry and overall flavor profile.

Variations

The berries used in my recipe were fresh strawberries, since they were readily available. Feel free to substitute with other berries, fresh or otherwise, such as blackberries, raspberries, blueberries or cherries. Dry ingredients such as chocolate chips, dried fruit or nuts may be added as well for more texture.

I used mascarpone since I had it on hand (as leftover from a rich tiramisu recipe). The original recipe used cream cheese, which is more economical and lower in calories, but calls for the addition of sugar when whipping. The mascarpone is a cheese that is already sweet, so I opted to add salt to balance the flavor. The cheese ended up being a thicker layer on top of the cake which added pockets of saltiness to balance the sweetness of the cake and sourness of the strawberries. Consider complementing your cheese topping to your fruit addition!

The crumb topping was a simple brown sugar and cinnamon combo, but other warm spices can be added in addition to the cinnamon such as, cardamom, allspice and nutmeg. For this recipe, I wanted to keep it simple so my star ingredient, the strawberries, would shine.
entry.summary: a dense, moist cake with cinnamon, fruit and cheese toppings

entry.title: brown butter whiskey
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for a whiskey fat-washed with brown butter for sipping on the rocks.

Materials

  • Light-colored pan
  • Silicone spatula
  • Optional: Funnel
  • 2 Glass Jars
  • 2 Cheesecloths
  • Coffee filter

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Butter 1 Cup Room temperature
Whiskey 500 mL None


Procedure

Prepare Brown Butter

Hands-on: 15 mins

  1. Heat a light-colored pan to medium heat on the stove.
  2. Cut softened butter into small, equally-sized slices.
  3. Once pan has heated up, add butter.
  4. Continuously stir with silicone spatula until cubes have melted.
  5. Listen for when the crackling subsides and foam starts to clear - milk solids (brown bits) will start forming on the bottom of the pan.
  6. Continue stirring for 10-20s.
  7. Immediately take off heat.
Prepare Infusion

Hands-on: 5 mins | Incubation: 24 h

  1. Add whiskey and hot brown butter to a glass jar. Use a funnel if needed.
  2. Swirl contents to mix.
  3. Leave on the counter for up to 12 h to allow contents to infuse. Swirl contents every hour or so to mix.
  4. Solid butter will separate from the whiskey. Allow contents to separate further by placing the jar in the freezer for at least 4 h.
Separate Infused Butter

Hands-on: 15 mins

  1. Take jar out of the freezer and allow butter to soften, about 15 mins.
  2. Place a funnel over a new jar. Line the funnel with 2 layers of cheesecloth.
  3. Pour the infusion through the funnel. Butter solids will be filtered by the cheesecloth.
  4. Squeeze the cheesecloth to remove any excess whiskey.
    • The infused butter may be stored for later use.
  5. Further filter the whiskey with a coffee filter place over a new jar.
  6. Serve the brown-butter infused whiskey over ice.
Yield 10 servings.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 months.


Discussion

Brown butter-washed whiskey. Photo from Unsplash.

In an attempt to make a peaty whiskey more palatable, I fat-washed it with brown butter. The resulting drink was a bit less peaty without the signature kick of spiciness. Overall, the drink was more pleasant to sip and though I’m not a whiskey drinker, the process is worth it alone for the infused butter! The butter was not completely removed from the whiskey when filtered with only 2 cheesecloths, which caused some white precipitation to settle on the bottom of the jar. When disturbed it would create swirls in the amber liquid and it was noted that the buttery mouthfeel degraded the drinking experience. If a coffee filter is on hand, then it is recommended to use the coffee filter after filtering with cheesecloth to remove particles that were initially able to flow through.

On the side, I had another experiment, where I took half the browned butter and added that to an already palatable Canadian maple syrup whiskey. The result was a sweet and buttery whiskey, a dangerous combination which I had to taste over and over to confirm that it was true! If you happen to find a bottle of Canadian maple syrup whiskey, do try this recipe.

Variations

Though this is only one variation of fat-washed alcohol, there are so many options to explore! Many different alcohols can be used, such as tequila, bourbon and vodka. Other fats such as animal fat or cooking oils can be substituted, though none will compare to the water content of butter. Infusion will be the same, though separation may need some adjusting for the time needed to solidify the fat.

Uses of these infusions can range wildly and will enhance your dishes or drinks! Check out my recipe for Whiskey Brown Butter!
entry.summary: a smooth fat-washed whiskey with nutty notes

entry.title: whiskey brown butter
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for a brown butter infusion with whiskey to be used for baking or cooking.

Materials

  • Light-colored pan
  • Silicone spatula
  • Optional: Funnel
  • 2 Glass Jars
  • 2 Cheesecloths

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Butter 1 Cup Room temperature
Whiskey 500 mL None


Procedure

Prepare Brown Butter

Hands-on: 15 mins

  1. Heat a light-colored pan to medium heat on the stove.
  2. Cut softened butter into small, equally-sized slices.
  3. Once pan has heated up, add butter.
  4. Continuously stir with silicone spatula until cubes have melted.
  5. Listen for when the crackling subsides and foam starts to clear - milk solids (brown bits) will start forming on the bottom of the pan.
  6. Continue stirring for 10-20s.
  7. Immediately take off heat.
Prepare Infusion

Hands-on: 5 mins | Incubation: 24 h

  1. Add whiskey and hot brown butter to a glass jar. Use a funnel if needed.
  2. Swirl contents to mix.
  3. Leave on the counter for up to 12 h to allow contents to infuse. Swirl contents every hour or so to mix.
  4. Solid butter will separate from the whiskey. Allow contents to separate further by placing the jar in the freezer for at least 4 h.
Separate Infused Butter

Hands-on: 15 mins

  1. Take jar out of the freezer and allow butter to soften, about 15 mins.
  2. Place a funnel over a new jar. Line the funnel with 2 layers of cheesecloth.
  3. Pour the infusion through the funnel. Butter solids will be filtered by the cheesecloth.
    • The infused whiskey may be stored for later use.
  4. Squeeze the cheesecloth to remove any excess whiskey.
  5. Store whiskey-infused brown butter for future recipes.
Yield A little over 1 cup of butter.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.


Discussion

Brown butter. Photo from Flikr.

Brown butter, the precious liquid gold, can be further elevated by infusing different flavors ito it. In this case, we are using whiskey (which was frankly too peaty for my taste) which will impart smokey and woody notes based on how it was stored. Alcohol has parts of it that are liquid soluble, and others that are fat soluble. This allows some flavors from the butter to dissolve in the whiskey, while others are captured by freezing the butter. A by-product of this process is a fat-washed whiskey which can be more flavorful and have an interesting mouthfeel.

Applications

The resulting whiskey-infused brown butter will contain more liquid than if we browned butter by itself. As such, recipes that are sensitive to changes in the ratio of wet to dry ingredients will need to account for this difference. For example, I made my classic brown butter chocolate chip cookies using whiskey butter and found that baking at 12 mins, which usually yields a soft, chewy cookie ended up being undercooked due to the additional liquid content from the whiskey. An adjustment to baking for 14 mins yielded the perfect texture. Other uses in baking includes buttercream frosting, cupcakes and pancakes.

Cooking with this butter will be a bit delicate since the toasted milk solids will continue to cook, then burn. The alcohol content will evaporate with high heat, though not completely, as a function of the temperature and length of cooking. I’d recommend adding the whiskey-infused brown butter at the end of cooking to impart the nutty, smoky flavors rather than frying with it.

Variations

Though this is only one variation of alcohol-infused fat, there are so many options to explore! Many different alcohols can be used, such as tequila, bourbon and vodka. Other fats such as animal fat or cooking oils can be substituted, though none will compare to the water content of butter. Infusion will be the same, though separation may need some adjusting for the time needed to solidify the fat.

Uses of these infusions can range wildly and will enhance your dishes! Check out my recipe for Brown Butter Whiskey!
entry.summary: a butter infusion with a smoky flavor

entry.title: fermented fries
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for fries with a fermented tang, reminiscent of vinegar and salt fries.

Materials

  • Large bowl
  • Fermentation container for fries (preferably glass)
  • Recommended: Kitchen scale
  • Kitchen Towel
  • Air fryer

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Potato, preferably russet 2 potatoes Washed
White vinegar or sauerkraut pickling juice 2 Tbsp None
Water, preferably filtered 500 mL None
Salt 15 g None
Optional: Garlic powder 1 Tbsp None
Optional: Chili powder 1/2 Tbsp None
Optional: Black pepper 1/2 Tbsp None
Optional: Sage 4 leaves Washed
Optional: Cabbage 1 leaf Washed
Cooking oil spray 2 Tbsp None


Procedure

Prepare Potato Sticks

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Cut potato into even matchsticks about 1/2 x 1/2” and place into a large bowl.
    • Cut potatoes as evenly as possible to ensure even cooking.
    • Potatoes may be cut thicker or thinner, cooking time will need to be adjusted accordingly.
  2. Submerge the sticks in water and gently agitate to wash the sticks.
  3. Pour out the starchy water and soak sticks in fresh water. Set aside.
Prepare Fermenting Brine

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. In a clean container, measure and pour 500 mL or 500 g of water.
  2. Add 2 Tbsp of white vinegar or sauerkraut pickling juice.
  3. Add 15 g of salt to make 3% brine. Add additional spices like garlic powder, chili powder, black pepper and sage to taste.
Ferment Potato Fries

Incubation: 3-7 days

  1. Add soaked potato sticks and fermenting brine to the fermenting container. Ensure sticks are completely submerged.
  2. Optional: Add a cabbage leaf to the fermenting container to prevent sticks from floating.
  3. Put the lid on loosely to allow gases to escape. Leave fermenting container in a cool, dark place for 3-7 days.
    • Tighten the lid and mix contents about once daily. Loosen the lid afterwards.
    • By day 3, you should observe some changes in the brine. The brine will appear cloudy and bubbles will float to the top if the jar is tapped. The potatoes are ready to be fried.
    • Potato sticks may be left to ferment longer, which will develop a stronger funkiness.
Frying Fermented Fries

Incubation: 20-30 mins + Optional 20 mins

  1. Preheat the air fryer to 375oF.
  2. Drain the brining liquid and dry the potato sticks with a towel.
    • Brine may be stored in the fridge for up to 1 month to be used as fermentation starter for future batches.
  3. Add the sticks to the pre-heated air fryer and spray with cooking oil.
  4. Cook for 20-30 mins or until golden brown. Shake the basket and spray with more oil every 10 mins.
  5. Optional: After cooking, let the fries cool either in the fridge or freezer for 15 mins. Bake again at 400oF for 5 mins.
    • This step allows the fries to crisp up even more.
Serve Fermented Fries
  1. Fries will taste salty, sour and garlicky, so additional toppings are not required.
  2. Serve fries with ketchup or mayo.
Yield 2 servings.
Storage Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week or in the freezer for up to 3 months.


Discussion

Fresh homemade fermented fries. Photo from Unsplash.

When tasting my first batch of fermented fries, I was instantly hooked and made several more batches. The potatoes slices are soaked in a flavorful brine which allows the flavors to really soak into the rest of the fry, not just the surface. The lactic acid produced by the fermentation created a subtle flavor which can be picked up in some but not all fries. Some were a little sour, some were downright funky, reminiscent of a stinky cheese. This flavor variance intrigued me and no matter how long I fermented my fries for, (3 vs 7 days) there were still some fries without any hint of funkiness.

Fermentation

Fermented fries are not so different from your typical French fries, with the main difference being the fermentation time. To make crispy French fries at home, the potato slices will need to be soaked in water anyway to remove excess starches. However, we add another purpose to this soaking with fermentation - and that is where the magic happens. The bacteria that naturally occurs on the skins of potatoes, cabbage leaves and sauerkraut pickling juice kick starts the fermentation process which produces the cloudy, sour brine after about 3 days. The bacteria break down complex carbohydrates into lactic acid through a process called Lactic Acid Fermentation. This acid by-product not only contributes to the unique flavor of fermented fries, but also aids in its preservation, as the acidic, low pH environment is no longer suitable for other bacteria species to grow.

Variations

In my take on fermented fries, I leaned heavily into the garlicky flavor profile for the brine. This paid off, as the garlic flavor was very strong after frying. This was inspired by a personal favorite take with garlic sage fries from Southern Pacific Brewing. Other favorite toppings to try adding to the brine are more spices (play around with chili flakes), fresh aromatics (rather than dried) and other herbs. Conversely, a plain brine is more than enough to produce delicious fermented fries.
entry.summary: a tangy spin on the classic french fries

entry.title: tofu in ginger syrup
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe with a spicy, gingery syrup and delicate, soft tofu topped with coconut cream.

Materials

  • Saucepan
  • Silicone spatula
  • Ladle
  • Dessert bowls and spoons

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Water 1 cup None
Dark brown sugar 1 cup None
Ginger 3” root Skin peeled, slice into matchsticks
Silken tofu 1 lb None
Coconut cream 4 Tbsp Heat and mix to emulsify


Procedure

Prepare Ginger Syrup

Hands-on: 10 mins | Incubation: 30 mins

  1. Heat water, brown sugar and ginger in a saucepot over medium-low heat. Stir with spatula until sugar is dissolved and syrup slightly thickens, approximately 5 mins.
  2. Take off heat and allow to cool for 30 mins.
    • Ginger syrup can be stored and further infused until ready to serve.
Serve Tofu

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Using a spoon, take thin slices of the tofu and place in serving bowl.
  2. Pour ginger syrup until tofu is barely submerged. Add ginger slices as well.
  3. Top with a tablespoon of coconut cream.
  4. Serve cold with ice or serve hot after microwaving for ~30s. Optionally, top with sesame seeds.
Yield 4 small bowls.
Storage Store the ginger syrup in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 month.


Discussion

Silken tofu in ginger syrup. Photo from FMT.

This recipe is a love letter to Vietnamese chè, or sweet soup. The spiciness of the ginger syrup complements the delicate texture of the silken tofu and the nuttiness of the coconut cream. A personal favorite dessert that takes no time at all to prepare and easy to store any leftovers. This dessert is unsurprisingly vegan, as most traditional chè are, featuring differing combinations of recurring simple ingredients.

Ginger Syrup

Ginger syrup is a staple in a lot of Vietnamese chè, so any leftover syrup may be stored in the fridge and used for another recipe. The unique flavor profile of the ginger syrup can be used in drinks such as lattes and cocktails to add a sweet, gingery note.

Variations

The simplicity of this tofu dessert brings back memories of savoring this dish warm from the stovetop. Other traditional toppings typically served with this dessert are glutinous rice balls with or without filling. These glutinous rice balls add a bit of chewiness to an otherwise soft texture. The filling can be sweet when filled with red bean or mung bean; or it can be savory when filled with black sesame or crushed peanuts. More modern variations of this dessert include tapioca balls, sago and chewy jellies.

entry.title: yuzu habanero pepper jelly
entry.content:
Abstract

A recipe for a jelly preserve that has a kick from the habanero pepper and a tang from the yuzu.

Heavily inspired by Katie’s recipe.

Materials

  • Recommended: food-safe powder-free gloves
  • Saucepan
  • Small bowl
  • Sterilized spoon
  • Sterilized canning jar (>14 oz)

Reagents

  Ingredient Amount Preparation
Habanero 1/4 Cup Washed
Bell pepper 1 Cup Finely chopped and deseeded
Distilled vinegar 1/2 Cup None
Yuzu extract 2 Tbsp None
Pectin (Optional: sugar-free) 1 oz None
Granulated Sugar 2 Cups or follow instructions on the pectin box None


Procedure

Prepare Habaneros

Hands-on: 5 mins

  1. Don gloves, wash gloves with soap.
  2. Using a knife and cutting board, slice habaneros in half. Remove seeds and stem.
  3. Finely chop habaneros. The smaller the strips, the quicker the habanero will cook.
  4. Set aside in a small bowl. Discard gloves.
Prepare Jelly

Hands-on: 15 mins

  1. In a saucepan on high heat, add habanero and bell peppers.
  2. In a small bowl, mix yuzu extract and pectin together. Mixture will be thick like cornstarch and water.
  3. Add the pectin mixture to the saucepan and stir continuously. Bring to a boil and remove from heat.
  4. Add sugar and place on high heat. Return to rolling boil for 1 min.
  5. Remove from heat and skim off any foam
  6. Add to sterilized jar.
Preserve Jelly

Hands-on: 10 mins | Incubation: 2+ days

  1. Add jar to a pot and completely submerge with hot water. Boil for 5-10 mins depending on altitude.
  2. Remove from heat.
  3. Test seal by pressing the center of the lid. If lid springs back, repeat boiling process.
  4. Allow jar to cool to room temperature, about 12 h.
    • Jelly will continue to thicken for 2 days at room temperature.
    • Jelly may be stored at room temperature or in the fridge where it will thicken even more.
  5. Store jar upside down so that peppers are floating to the bottom of the jar.
  6. After 2 days, store jar right side up. Peppers in the jelly will be distributed evenly instead of floating to the top.
Serve Jelly
  1. Unseal the jar. You should hear a pop which indicates that the seal is still effective.
  2. Serve on toast or with crackers and cheese.
Yield 1 14 oz jar.
Storage Preserved jelly is shelf-stable for 3 years. Refrigerate after opening for up to 1 month.


Discussion

Jars of pepper jelly. Photo from Wikimedia.

Yuzu habanero pepper jelly was surprisingly a hit, as there was heat from the habanero, which was tempered by the sourness of the yuzu and sweetness of the jelly. A perfect addition to wine and cheese night. The jelly set soft and slightly runny from room temperature, but was the perfect thickness after a night of setting in the fridge. If you prefer a thicker jelly, try using sugar-free pectin or more sugar.

Variations

To my orange habaneros, I added yellow and orange bell peppers to keep with the same color scheme for a palette that was harmonious to the eyes. If that’s not a consideration for you, feel free to add any combination of hot peppers and bell peppers to your jelly.

To temper the spiciness, fruits may be added as well. Some fruits that go well with peppers are mango, strawberry and blueberry. The fruit will add a hint of sweetness to balance out the spicy heat of the peppers.

The acid in the jelly can be substituted as well. I used a combination of distilled vinegar and yuzu since I did not have apple cider vinegar on hand. The yuzu mimiced the depth of flavor I would be missing from the apple cider vinegar and added a slightly herbal, citrus note to the jelly without being too overpowering.

Spice Level

I chose habaneros, a pepper with a rating of 100-350k Scoville Heat Units (SCU) which is on the spicier side, since it was readily available to me for free at a farmer’s market. The resulting heat in the jelly was surprisingly bearable (coming from someone with a mild spice tolerance). Cooking down the peppers will reduce the heat, so the time cooked may be adjusted based on desired spice level. Yes, my tongue and mouth still burned, but it was nothing like the heat I felt after slicing the habaneros, washing my hands (3 times!) and touching my face - please be careful when handling peppers!

For comparison, here are the SCUs of some commonly eaten peppers:

Pepper Spiciness (SCU)
Bell pepper 0
Jalapeno pepper 2.5-10k
Cayenne pepper 25-50K
Thai chilies 50-100k
Habanero pepper 100k-350K
entry.summary: a sweet and spicy jelly preserve
